items.e: The produce of the fourth year ( neta reva'i ) is holy, as [Leviticus 19:24] states: "And in its fourth year, all of its produce shall be holy, consecrated unto God." The law applying to it is that it must be eaten in Jerusalem by its owners in the same way as the second tithe. Just as the laws of the second tithe do not apply in Syria, so too, the laws of neta reva'i do not apply in Syria. With regard to neta reva'i , [Numbers 5:10] states: "A person's consecrated property shall be his." For there is no other consecrated property about which the Torah does not inform to whom it should be given with the exception of neta reva'i .

A person who desires to redeem neta reva'i should redeem it in the same manner as which he redeems the produce of the second tithe. If he redeems it for his own self, he must add a fifth [to its value]. It may not be redeemed until it reaches the "phase of tithing," as [implied by Leviticus 19:25]: "To increase its produce for you," [i.e., these laws do not apply] until [the crops] have become produce. [ Neta reva'i ] may not be redeemed while it is attached [to the ground], as is the law with regard to the second tithe. And it is the property of the Most High, as is the second tithe. Therefore, it cannot be acquired when given as a present unless it was given when it was not yet ripe. With regard to other matters, e.g., eating, drinking, and redemption, the laws that apply to it are those applying to the second tithe.

When a person redeems a vineyard in its fourth year of growth, he may redeem it as grapes or he may redeem it as wine. Similarly, olives [may be redeemed as fruit or as oil]. Other fruits, by contrast, may only be redeemed in their natural state.

The laws of shichachah, pe'ah, peret, and ollelot do not apply to a vineyard that is in its fourth year. Nor should terumah and the tithes be separated from it, as they are not separated from the second tithe. Instead, it should be brought to Jerusalem in its entirety or redeemed and the money taken to Jerusalem [and used for food there] like the second tithe.

Our Sages ordained that grapes from a vineyard in its fourth year from a radius of a one-day journey from Jerusalem should be brought there to embellish the marketplaces of Jerusalem with fruit. After the Temple was destroyed, it may be redeemed even directly outside the city's wall. Other types of produce may be redeemed even directly outside the city's wall even during the time the Temple was standing.

How is neta reva'i redeemed? One should evaluate [the size of] a basket [of fruit] through the agency of three men who estimate how much produce would a person [want] for a sela that he would pay for this fruit when it is considered that [in addition] he would have to pay the cost of watchmen, donkey-drivers, and workers. After the rate is established, he should place down the money and say: "The holiness of all [the produce] gathered from this [orchard] is transferred to this money," estimating how many baskets worth a sela [the orchard] contains. In the Sabbatical year, he should redeem [the produce of the orchard] for its worth. For in that year, there are no watchmen or workers [to pay]. If [the orchard] was declared ownerless, all that is necessary to deduct is the wages for gathering it.

When a person had [an orchard that was in] its fourth year of growth in the Sabbatical year when everyone is allowed equal access to it, he must mark it with mounds of earth so that [those who take the produce] will recognize [its sacred quality] and not partake of it until they redeem it. If [the produce is] within the [three] orlah years, it should be marked with baked clay so that [people] will shun it. [We use clay instead of mounds of earth], lest the latter crumble. [The rationale is that] the prohibition of orlah is more severe, because benefit from it is forbidden. Those who are meticulous in their observance of the Torah's prohibitions would set aside money in the Sabbatical year and say: "The holiness of everything harvested from these fruits of the fourth year is transferred to this money." [The redemption must be carried out in this fashion,] because it is forbidden to redeem [the produce] while it is attached to the ground, as explained.

The first of Tishrei is the beginning of the year with regard to the reckoning of orlah and neta reva'i . When do we begin counting the year with regard to these prohibitions? From the time the trees are planted. [A year does not have to be] from Rosh HaShanah to Rosh HaShanah. Instead, 30 days within a year are considered a year. [This applies] provided the planting takes root before these thirty days [begin]. How long does it take? Generally, the time for all trees to take root is two weeks.

Thus when a person plants a tree 44 days before Rosh HaShanah, it is considered as if the tree had been planted for an entire year. Nevertheless, due to the prohibition of orlah , in the fourth year, the fruit from this planting is not permitted until the fifteenth of Shvat, which is "the New Year of the Trees."

What is implied? When a person plants a fruit tree on the fifteenth of Av of the tenth year in the Jubilee cycle, it is considered as being orlah until the fifteenth of Shvat of the thirteenth year of the Jubilee cycle. Whatever fruit produced by the tree during this time is orlah , even though it did not ripen until several days after [that date]. From the fifteenth of Shvat from the thirteenth year of the Jubilee cycle until the fifteenth of Shvat of the fourteenth year, the produce is neta reva'i . Whatever fruit produced during this time is neta reva'i and must be redeemed. If the year is declared a leap year, [the produce grown in] the extra month is considered as orlah or neta reva'i .

If it was planted on the sixteenth of Av in the tenth year, the tenth year is not reckoned for it. Instead, it is orlah throughout the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth years. And it is neta reva'i from Rosh HaShanah of the fourteenth year until its conclusion.

If one planted the tree between the first of Tishrei and the fifteenth of Shvat, he should count three years from day to day for orlah and [four years] from day to day for neta reva'i . I have seen Geonim who have a different approach regarding the reckoning of orlah and neta reva'i . It is not appropriate to elaborate in rebuttal of them. Theirs is a scholarly error and we have already outlined the true path.

Leaves, blossoms, sap, and fruit buds, are permitted in [the years of] orlah and neta reva'i . Grapes that were devastated by the west wind and ruined, grape seeds, grape peels, water mixed with grape dregs, the peels of pomegranates, their flowers, the shells of nuts, and seeds within a fruit are forbidden with regard to orlah and permitted with regard to neta reva'i . Fruit that withers and falls from the tree are forbidden in all instances.
